systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.

Titre d'origine : Reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material have surged more than 8,400 percent in two years

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (The Decoder) :
Reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material have surged more than 8,400 percent in two years
Reports of AI being used for the sexual exploitation of children have jumped more than 8,400 percent in two years. According to a report by Edinburgh's Childlight Institute, the number of reported AI-generated abuse images climbed from about 4,700 in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025, The Guardian reports. The material includes AI-manipulated images (deepfakes) from so-called "nudify apps" that digitally strip people of their clothing. Abusers can use the faked images to blackmail children into handing over money or more photos.
The data comes from reports that tech companies filed with the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). The UK's Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) reviewed 6,310 criminal, photorealistic AI-generated abuse images in the first half of 2026 alone. That's 40 percent more than in all of 2025.
Childlight data director Debi Fry acknowledges that better detection systems partly explain the spike. She still calls for swift action from lawmakers and tech companies. Childlight CEO Paul Stanfield wants governments to classify the problem as a preventable public health emergency, dedicate funding to prevention, and coordinate efforts across healthcare, schools, child protection services, and the justice system.

SOURCE 2 (shattered.io) :
Technology companies filed more than 400,000 reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material with the U.S. National Center for Missing and Exploited Children in 2025. In 2023 the figure was about 4,700. That is a rise of more than 8,400% in two years, according to Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute, a research center hosted at the University of Edinburgh, as The Guardian reported.
The scale of the change is what stands out. A category that barely registered in 2023 now fills hundreds of thousands of filings a year. The numbers arrive as pressure on platforms keeps building, a pattern we tracked in our report on Big Tech’s online safety record. This analysis walks through what the data confirms, what it leaves open, and what it means for AI developers, platforms and families.
One note on handling. The subject is grim, so this piece keeps to the statistics, the sourcing and the policy questions. It does not describe the material itself. Every figure below comes from the Childlight work as covered by The Guardian or from the Internet Watch Foundation. Where we do our own arithmetic or draw our own conclusions, we say so.
What Childlight Found in the NCMEC Report Data
Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute analyzed reports that technology companies submitted to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, the U.S. clearinghouse for suspected child exploitation material. The headline result is a climb from roughly 4,700 AI-related reports in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.
Two details define the dataset. First, it counts reports from technology companies, not convictions, arrests or individual victims. Second, the material in those reports includes AI-generated deepfake images and images made with so-called nudify applications. Those are the two categories the coverage names explicitly.
Childlight sits inside a university setting, which matters for how readers weigh the work. It is a research institute, not a regulator and not a platform. Its role here is to aggregate and interpret reporting data that would otherwise stay scattered across company filings. The Guardian presented the 8,400% figure as the central finding, and the underlying counts support it.
The Numbers at a Glance
The table below collects every confirmed figure from the two datasets covered in this story. We list the source next to each number so readers can see which organization stands behind it.
Read the table in two layers. The first three rows describe volume of reporting to a U.S. clearinghouse. The remaining rows describe what one UK-based hotline verified and classified. They measure different things, which explains why one number is up 8,400% and the other is up 14%.
How 4,700 Became 400,000: Reading the 8,400% Figure
The math checks out. Going from about 4,700 to more than 400,000 is a multiple of roughly 85. Subtract the starting value, divide by it, and you land just above 8,400%. Because the 2025 number is stated as “more than” 400,000, the real increase sits at or above that mark.
What the figure measures
The figure tracks filings by technology companies. A filing means a company flagged content and passed it to NCMEC. It does not equal the number of children harmed, the number of offenders, or the number of distinct images. The reporting we have does not break down how many files each filing contained, so we cannot convert reports into images.
What the figure cannot tell us
Several forces could push a reporting count up. More material could be circulating. Companies could be detecting more of what already existed. More firms could have started reporting at all. Our reading is that all three likely play a part, but the published data does not separate them. Readers should treat the 8,400% number as a measure of what reached the reporting pipeline, not as a clean measure of how much material exists.
That caveat does not shrink the finding. Even if better detection explained a large share of the rise, a jump from the low thousands to several hundred thousand means the pipeline now handles a volume it did not face two years ago. Investigators, hotlines and platform safety teams have to absorb that load.
Deepfakes and Nudify Apps Drive Much of the Concern
According to the coverage of the Childlight study, the reported material includes AI-generated deepfake images and images produced with nudify applications. Nudify apps are tools that claim to digitally remove clothing from a photograph. Deepfakes more broadly are synthetic images or video that place a real person’s likeness into fabricated content.
Both categories raise a problem that older forms of abuse material did not. A photograph of a real child can feed the tools, which means a victim can exist without any original abuse ever being recorded. Lawmakers and safety groups have argued for years that such material still harms the people depicted, and the volume now showing up in reports suggests the concern has moved from theory to routine casework.
The sources we reviewed do not say how the reports split between deepfakes, nudify output and fully synthetic images. They also do not name any specific app, model or company. We will not guess. Any claim that ties a particular product to this surge needs its own evidence, and none of it appears in the confirmed material.
The question of how AI products handle minors is already reaching courts. For a related case study, see our coverage of the Gemini lawsuit over a school monitoring gap, which shows how quickly child-safety questions around AI systems turn into litigation.
Which Regions the Study Covered
The Childlight study covered East Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Earlier research from the same institute examined Western Europe. Together those pieces give a partial map rather than a global one.
The coverage names no other regions. That leaves open how the pattern looks in places the reporting does not mention. We cannot say those places are better or worse off. We can say the evidence does not reach them yet.
The regional spread still carries a message. Three very different parts of the world, with different languages, laws and internet habits, appear in one study. When a problem shows up across that range, it points toward a technology-driven cause rather than a local one. Image generation tools do not respect borders, and neither do the platforms that host and report the output.
The Internet Watch Foundation’s Separate Count
The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) offers a second lens. In 2025 it identified 8,029 AI-generated images and videos depicting realistic child sexual abuse. That is a 14% increase from the previous year. By our arithmetic, a 14% rise to 8,029 implies a 2024 total of roughly 7,000, though the IWF’s own prior-year figure should be treated as the authoritative number.
The gap between 14% and 8,400% looks like a contradiction, but it is not. The IWF counts material its analysts found and verified as realistic. Childlight counts reports that companies sent to NCMEC. One is a quality-controlled tally by a hotline. The other is a firehose measure of filings. A filing count can explode while a verified-content count grows at a steadier pace, especially when automated detection feeds the first and human review limits the second.
The word “realistic” matters too. The IWF figure concerns material that looks real enough to be treated as depicting actual abuse. As image quality improves, the line between synthetic and photographic content blurs, which makes analyst workloads heavier and verification slower.
Video Is the Fastest-Moving Format
The sharpest single data point in the IWF release concerns video. The hotline identified 3,443 AI-generated child sexual abuse videos in 2025. In 2024 it identified 13. That is more than a 260-fold increase, and it arrived within one calendar year.
Video generation lagged image generation for most of the recent AI boom. Moving pictures demand more computing power and more skill to keep consistent from frame to frame. The IWF numbers suggest that barrier has fallen quickly. Our interpretation is that the format gap closed because the tools improved, but the IWF figures themselves do not name a cause.
Analysts also read video differently from stills. A clip takes longer to review, can carry more distressing detail, and can be harder to trace back to a source. A jump from 13 files to 3,443 therefore adds a heavier burden per item than the raw count suggests.
Debate over who can build and release powerful generative models runs through this issue. Open-weight systems face particular scrutiny, a tension we explored in our piece on Hugging Face’s warning about two attacks that could close open AI. The data here does not say which kinds of models produced the material, so it cannot settle that argument either way.
Category A: What the 65% Severity Figure Means
The IWF classified 65% of those 3,443 videos as Category A, its most severe category. Applying that share gives about 2,240 videos, which is our own calculation rather than a published count.
The point of the severity tier is to show where the harm concentrates. A majority of the AI-generated videos fell into the worst grading. Nobody should read the synthetic origin of the files as a sign of milder content. By the IWF’s own classification, most of the video material sat at the top of the scale.
For policymakers, that undercuts a common assumption that AI-made material is less serious because no camera captured an event. The grading looks at what the content depicts, and by that standard the AI-generated videos skewed toward the extreme end.
Childlight vs IWF: Two Datasets Compared
Readers will meet both sets of figures in headlines, often mixed together. The comparison below keeps them apart. Use it before quoting either number.
Neither dataset invalidates the other. The Childlight numbers show how heavily the reporting system now feels AI content. The IWF numbers show what verified, realistic material looks like once humans review it, and how severe the video share has become. Used together they point the same way, even though the percentages differ wildly.
Historical Context: From Rare Edge Case to Mass Reporting
Child safety groups warned about generative AI and abuse material almost as soon as image generators reached the public. Early warnings were mostly forward-looking. The 2023 baseline of roughly 4,700 reports to NCMEC reflects that early stage, when the issue existed but sat at the margins of the reporting system.
Two years later the margin became the mainstream of a growing queue. The IWF video numbers make the shift vivid. With only 13 AI-generated videos identified in 2024, video barely existed as a category. One year on, it reached 3,443 and carried a majority of Category A content.
Regulators have been catching up to harm that moves this quickly. Europe’s debate over a Digital Fairness Act shows how contested new obligations get once industry weighs in, as we covered in our report on trade bodies calling the 6% fines unworkable. That fight concerns consumer protection broadly, but it illustrates the pace problem. Technology compounds in months while legislation takes years.
Market Impact: What This Means for AI Developers and Platforms
The sources do not quantify financial fallout, and we will not invent figures. The direction of travel is still clear enough to describe. Data like this raises the cost of doing business for anyone who builds, hosts or distributes image and video generation tools.
Trust and safety budgets are the first pressure point. Companies that file reports need detection systems, reviewers and legal staff to handle volumes in the hundreds of thousands. Firms that stay quiet risk being the ones regulators single out when the next dataset lands.
Litigation risk is the second. Advocacy groups already use the courts to push AI developers on safety, as in the nonprofit complaint against five AI developers. That case targets frontier AI broadly, not this specific problem. Still, a documented 8,400% rise gives plaintiffs and regulators a concrete number to cite in any future action over child safety.
App distribution is the third. Nudify applications are named in the reporting, and app stores, payment processors and hosting providers sit between those tools and their users. Expect intermediaries to face more questions about what they allow. For wider context on where AI governance is heading, our AI and machine learning section tracks the policy and product moves as they happen.
What Is Confirmed and What Is Not
Precision matters here more than usual. Loose claims about child abuse material spread fast and can unfairly implicate companies or individuals. The table separates what the sources support from what they do not.
The bottom two rows deserve emphasis. No source we reviewed names a tool, firm or person as the driver of the surge. Anyone asserting otherwise is going beyond the evidence.
Five Predictions for the Next 12 Months
These are our forecasts, not reported facts. They rest on the direction of the confirmed data and carry real uncertainty.
- Reporting volumes keep climbing. With 2025 already above 400,000, we expect the 2026 count to exceed it, though the rate of growth should slow from the 8,400% two-year jump simply because the base is now large.
- Video becomes the main battleground. A move from 13 to 3,443 videos in one year leaves little reason to expect a pause. Detection tools tuned for still images will need retraining for moving content.
- Regulators cite these figures directly. Hearings, consultations and enforcement notices tend to quote the largest available number. Expect the 8,400% figure to appear in policy documents.
- Pressure shifts to intermediaries. App stores, payment providers and hosts will face tougher questions about nudify applications, since the reporting names those tools.
- More research fills the geographic gaps. The study covers three regions plus earlier Western Europe work. Pressure will grow for similar analysis in regions the coverage does not mention.
The wild card is measurement. If companies change how they classify or file reports, year-over-year comparisons could shift for reasons unrelated to the underlying problem. Watch for methodology notes when the next datasets land.
How Parents, Schools and Readers Should Respond
Statistics at this scale can leave families feeling helpless. A few steps still help. Talk with children early about nudify apps and deepfakes, including the fact that someone can make a fake image from an ordinary photo and that the child is never to blame.
If you come across suspected child sexual abuse material online, do not download, forward or screenshot it. Report it to the platform and to the proper hotline, such as NCMEC in the United States or the Internet Watch Foundation in the UK. Both organizations accept reports from the public.
